title: Postgres WAL & Replication: A Field Handbook
summary: A dense, practical tour of Postgres durability and replication — from WAL records and checkpoints through streaming replicas, synchronous commit levels, replication slots, logical decoding, and failover. Covers internals, configuration, trade-offs, and the mistakes that take clusters down.

chapters.title: WAL Fundamentals: Write-Ahead Logging
points: WAL rule: a change must be flushed to the log before the modified data page may be written to disk — durability without fsyncing every heap page.
Every modification (INSERT/UPDATE/DELETE/DDL/index change) emits a WAL record describing the physical page change, not the SQL statement.
WAL record anatomy: XLogRecord header (total length, xid, prev LSN, CRC-32C), resource manager ID, info flags, block references, and payload data.
Resource managers (rmgr): Heap, Btree, Gin, Gist, Transaction, XLOG, Standby, Sequence — each knows how to redo its own record type.
LSN (Log Sequence Number) = a 64-bit byte offset into the infinite WAL stream, printed as X/YYYYYYYY (e.g. 3F/A2B10C48); it is the universal clock of replication.
WAL is stored as 16 MB segment files (default) under pg_wal/, named by 24 hex chars = timelineID + logical log + segment number.
wal_buffers holds WAL in shared memory; it is flushed to disk on commit, on buffer pressure, or by the WAL writer process.
COMMIT is durable when its WAL record is fsync'd — commit cost is one sequential log write, not many random data writes.
Checkpoint: flushes all dirty shared buffers to data files and writes a checkpoint record; recovery only needs to replay WAL from the last checkpoint's redo pointer.

full_page_writes: the first change to a page after a checkpoint writes the entire 8 KB page image into WAL, protecting against torn pages after a crash — the main reason WAL volume spikes right after a checkpoint.
Crash recovery = REDO only: replay WAL forward from the redo point; uncommitted transactions are undone by MVCC visibility, not by an UNDO log (unlike Oracle/InnoDB).
wal_level values: minimal (no archiving/replication), replica (default, supports streaming + PITR), logical (adds row-level decoding info).
Inspect with pg_current_wal_lsn(), pg_walinspect (PG15+), or pg_waldump -p pg_wal 000000010000003F000000A2 to read raw records.
Common gotcha: fsync=off or full_page_writes=off make benchmarks fly and make crash recovery produce a silently corrupt cluster.

chapters.title: WAL Mechanics: Segments, Checkpoints, Archiving
points: Checkpoint triggers: checkpoint_timeout elapsed (default 5min), max_wal_size exceeded, manual CHECKPOINT, or clean shutdown.
checkpoint_completion_target (default 0.9) spreads the flush over most of the interval to avoid an I/O spike; raise checkpoint_timeout to 15–30min on busy systems to cut full-page-write volume.
max_wal_size is a soft target, not a hard cap — WAL can exceed it if checkpoints cannot keep up or a slot pins segments.
min_wal_size keeps recycled segments preallocated so steady-state writes reuse files instead of creating them.
WAL recycling: after a checkpoint, obsolete segments are renamed to future names rather than deleted, avoiding filesystem churn.
archive_mode = on plus archive_command (or archive_library for PG15+) copies each completed segment offsite; return nonzero on failure so Postgres retries.
Archiving rule: archive_command must never overwrite an existing file and must fsync — 'test ! -f dst && cp src dst' is the classic (and minimum) form.
A failing archive_command is a disk-fill bomb: Postgres refuses to recycle unarchived segments and pg_wal grows until the volume is full and the server PANICs.
Base backup + archived WAL = PITR: restore, set restore_command and recovery_target_time, and let recovery replay forward.
pg_basebackup -D dir -X stream -c fast -P takes a consistent base backup and streams the WAL generated during it.
Timelines: each promotion/PITR bumps the timelineID and writes a .history file, so a new branch of WAL cannot be confused with the old one.
archive_timeout forces a segment switch after N seconds so a low-traffic cluster's RPO isn't 16 MB of unarchived data.
wal_compression = on/lz4/zstd compresses full-page images, often halving WAL volume on write-heavy OLTP.
Monitor: pg_stat_bgwriter / pg_stat_checkpointer (PG17+) for checkpoints_req vs checkpoints_timed — a high requested ratio means max_wal_size is too small.

chapters.title: Streaming Replication: How a Replica Follows
points: Physical streaming replication ships raw WAL bytes; the replica is a byte-identical block-level copy, same page layout, same file names.
Processes: on the primary a walsender per connected replica; on the replica a walreceiver plus the startup process that applies the records.
Protocol: replica connects with replication=true, sends START_REPLICATION at an LSN, receives a continuous CopyBoth stream of WAL.
Bootstrap: pg_basebackup -h primary -D /data -R -X stream -S slotname -C writes standby.signal and primary_conninfo automatically.
standby.signal file (PG12+) puts the server in standby mode; recovery.conf is gone — its settings are now normal postgresql.conf GUCs.
primary_conninfo needs a role with the REPLICATION attribute and a matching pg_hba.conf line of type 'replication'.
Hot standby: hot_standby = on lets the replica serve read-only queries while continuously applying WAL.
The four LSN stages a replica reports: sent → write → flush → replay, exposed as sent_lsn/write_lsn/flush_lsn/replay_lsn in pg_stat_replication.
Lag measurement: pg_wal_lsn_diff(pg_current_wal_lsn(), replay_lsn) for bytes; write_lag/flush_lag/replay_lag columns for time.
A replica is read-only: any write raises 'cannot execute INSERT in a read-only transaction'; sequences, temp tables, and VACUUM are all blocked too.
Cascading replication: a standby can itself be a walsender for downstream standbys, reducing load and WAN fanout on the primary.
Restart safety: restore_command on a standby lets it fall back to the archive when the primary has already recycled a needed segment.
wal_receiver_status_interval controls how often the replica reports its position; hot_standby_feedback sends its oldest xmin upstream.
Delayed replica: recovery_min_apply_delay = '1h' keeps a standby deliberately behind as a human-error undo button.
Diagnostic pair: pg_stat_replication on the primary (one row per walsender), pg_stat_wal_receiver on the replica.

chapters.title: Synchronous vs Asynchronous Commit
points: Async (default): the primary commits as soon as its own WAL is fsync'd; replicas may lag, so failover can lose the last transactions.
Sync: COMMIT blocks until the named standby confirms the required stage — zero data loss at the cost of a network round trip per commit.
synchronous_commit levels, weakest to strongest: off, local, remote_write, on, remote_apply.
off = don't even wait for the local fsync (up to wal_writer_delay×3 of loss on crash, but never corruption); local = local fsync only, ignore standbys.
remote_write = standby has written to the OS but not fsync'd — survives a Postgres crash on the standby, not an OS/host crash.
on = standby has fsync'd the WAL (durable), the usual sync setting; remote_apply = standby has replayed it, so read-your-writes works on the replica.
synchronous_standby_names selects who counts: 'FIRST 1 (a, b, c)' uses priority order; 'ANY 2 (a, b, c)' is quorum commit (PG10+).
The setting is per-transaction: SET synchronous_commit = 'local' inside a bulk-load session while keeping the cluster default at 'on'.
Latency math: sync commit costs at least one RTT; a 5 ms cross-AZ RTT caps a single session at ~200 commits/sec no matter how fast the disks are.
The availability trap: with FIRST 1 (a) and only one sync standby, losing that standby stalls every commit on the primary — always configure N+1 candidates.
Canceling a waiting sync commit (Ctrl-C) is dangerous: the transaction is already committed locally and will appear after crash recovery, so the client gets an ambiguous answer.
Sync replication protects durability, not availability — it does not automatically fail over, and it does not protect against a bug that deletes data on the primary.
Comparison row — Async: fastest, RPO > 0, no primary stall. Sync (on): RPO = 0, RTT-bound, primary stalls if quorum unreachable.
Sane hybrid: ANY 1 of two local standbys for durability, plus a third async cross-region replica for disaster recovery.

chapters.title: Replication Slots: Guaranteed Retention
points: A slot is server-side state recording the oldest LSN a consumer still needs, so the primary refuses to remove that WAL.
Without a slot, a replica that disconnects too long hits: 'requested WAL segment ... has already been removed' and must be rebuilt.
Two kinds: physical slots (for streaming standbys, track restart_lsn) and logical slots (for decoding, also track confirmed_flush_lsn and a catalog xmin).
Create: SELECT pg_create_physical_replication_slot('replica1'); use it via primary_slot_name = 'replica1' on the standby.
Drop: SELECT pg_drop_replication_slot('replica1') — only when inactive; an active slot cannot be dropped.
Inspect pg_replication_slots: active, restart_lsn, confirmed_flush_lsn, wal_status (reserved/extended/unreserved/lost), safe_wal_size.
The #1 production outage from slots: an abandoned slot pins WAL forever and fills pg_wal until the disk is full and the primary shuts down.
max_slot_wal_keep_size (PG13+) caps retention per slot; past the cap the slot is invalidated (wal_status = 'lost') — bounded disk loss instead of an outage.
Logical slots also hold back the catalog xmin, blocking VACUUM from cleaning system catalogs and causing bloat plus transaction-ID wraparound risk.
wal_keep_size is the slotless alternative: keep N megabytes of WAL for everyone, best-effort, no guarantee and no disk-fill risk.
Slots are not replicated to standbys by default; before PG17 a slot vanished on failover, breaking every logical subscriber.
PG17 adds failover slots (failover = true plus sync_replication_slots on the standby) so logical slots survive promotion.
Slots are physical-file state in pg_replslot/, not WAL contents — they survive restart but are not included in a base backup's role.
Alert rule to always ship: warn when any slot is inactive AND pg_wal_lsn_diff(pg_current_wal_lsn(), restart_lsn) exceeds a few GB.

chapters.title: Logical Replication & Logical Decoding
points: Logical replication ships row-level changes (INSERT/UPDATE/DELETE tuples) decoded from WAL, not physical blocks — so target rows, not whole clusters.
Logical decoding reassembles WAL into a transaction-ordered change stream via an output plugin: pgoutput (built in), test_decoding, wal2json.
Requires wal_level = logical on the publisher and a logical replication slot per subscription.
Publisher side: CREATE PUBLICATION mypub FOR TABLE orders, customers; or FOR ALL TABLES; publish = 'insert,update,delete,truncate' filters operations.
Subscriber side: CREATE SUBSCRIPTION mysub CONNECTION 'host=... dbname=...' PUBLICATION mypub; — it creates the slot and starts an initial COPY.
REPLICA IDENTITY decides how UPDATE/DELETE identify a row: DEFAULT = primary key, FULL = whole old row (slow, seq-scan per change), NOTHING = updates/deletes fail.
A table with no primary key and no REPLICA IDENTITY FULL raises 'cannot update table ... because it does not have a replica identity'.
Not replicated: DDL, sequence values (until PG16 sequence sync), large objects, and TRUNCATE unless published — schema changes must be applied manually on both sides.
Both sides are writable, so conflicts are real: a duplicate key on the subscriber stops apply until you skip the LSN (ALTER SUBSCRIPTION ... SKIP) or fix the row.
Initial sync copies each table with a temporary slot; large tables can be excluded with copy_data = false when you seed them yourself.
PG14+ streams in-progress transactions (streaming = on) so a huge transaction doesn't buffer entirely on the publisher before sending.
Row filters (PG15) and column lists let a publication ship only WHERE region = 'eu' or only non-PII columns.
Killer use case: major-version upgrade with near-zero downtime — replicate PG13 → PG16 logically, then cut over the application.
Monitor pg_stat_subscription (received_lsn, latest_end_lsn) on the subscriber and pg_replication_slots on the publisher.
Comparison row — Physical: whole cluster, same version/arch, replica read-only, tiny overhead. Logical: per-table, cross-version, target writable, decoding CPU cost.

chapters.title: Replicas as Read Workhorses: Conflicts & Consistency
points: Read scaling: route reporting and analytics to hot standbys, but never assume a replica is current — it is eventually consistent by design.
Recovery conflict: WAL replay wants to remove a row version that a long-running query on the replica still needs to see.
The five conflict types: snapshot (cleaned-up tuples), lock (conflicting AccessExclusiveLock), tablespace, buffer pin, and deadlock.
Symptom: 'ERROR: canceling statement due to conflict with recovery / User query might have needed to see row versions that must be removed'.
max_standby_streaming_delay controls how long replay pauses before killing the query; -1 waits forever and lets the replica lag unboundedly.
hot_standby_feedback = on tells the primary the replica's oldest xmin so VACUUM keeps those row versions — trades primary bloat for replica query survival.
The hot_standby_feedback tax: a forgotten idle-in-transaction session on a replica can block VACUUM cluster-wide and bloat the primary.
Read-your-writes on a replica: use synchronous_commit = remote_apply, or capture pg_current_wal_insert_lsn() after the write and poll pg_last_wal_replay_lsn() on the replica.
Replay is single-threaded (one startup process), so a replica can fall behind a heavily parallel write workload no matter how fast its disk is.
pg_is_in_recovery() returns true on a standby — the standard cheap probe for connection routers and health checks.
target_session_attrs=read-write / read-only in libpq lets a single multi-host conninfo find the right node automatically.
Pause and resume replay with pg_wal_replay_pause() / pg_wal_replay_resume() to take a stable snapshot for a long report.
Replicas cannot create temp tables or write work files to tables — some ORMs and BI tools will fail on a standby for this reason alone.
Backups from a replica offload I/O from the primary, but need a slot or archive access so needed WAL is not recycled mid-backup.

chapters.title: Failover & High Availability
points: Promotion: pg_ctl promote (or SELECT pg_promote()) ends recovery, bumps the timeline, and makes the standby a writable primary.
Switchover = planned and lossless (stop writes, wait for full catch-up, promote, re-point). Failover = unplanned and may lose async transactions.
RPO = how much data you can lose (async: seconds; sync: zero). RTO = how long you're down (detection + promotion + client re-routing).
Split brain: two nodes both accepting writes after a network partition — the worst outcome, worse than downtime, and requires fencing/STONITH to prevent.
Quorum is the defense: an odd number of voting members and a witness so a minority partition demotes itself instead of promoting.
Postgres ships no automatic failover — you need Patroni (etcd/Consul-based, the de-facto standard), repmgr, or a cloud-managed control plane.
Patroni model: each node holds a DCS leader key with a TTL; losing the key means demote, holding it means renew — the DCS, not the DBA, arbitrates.
Client re-routing options: VIP, HAProxy health check on pg_is_in_recovery(), a service DNS record, or libpq multi-host with target_session_attrs.
Old primaries must be rewound, not just restarted: pg_rewind resyncs a diverged ex-primary against the new one without a full base backup.
pg_rewind requires wal_log_hints = on (or data checksums) and a clean shutdown of the source node.
After promotion the other standbys must follow the new timeline: point primary_conninfo at the new leader and restart (PG12+ can follow across a timeline switch).
Trigger-file promotion (promote_trigger_file) is deprecated in PG16 — use pg_ctl promote or pg_promote() instead.
Cascading standbys automatically follow their upstream's timeline change, so the topology below the promoted node survives.
Rehearse failover on a schedule; the failover you've never tested is the failover that discovers your pg_hba.conf lacks the new node.

chapters.title: Trade-offs, Tuning & Comparisons
points: Physical vs logical, one line: physical is byte-exact, whole-cluster, low overhead; logical is selective, cross-version, and costs CPU to decode and apply.
Sync vs async, one line: sync buys RPO = 0 and pays one RTT per commit; async buys latency and pays with a data-loss window.
Slot vs wal_keep_size: slots guarantee retention and risk disk fill; wal_keep_size is best-effort and risks a broken replica — max_slot_wal_keep_size is the middle ground.
Streaming vs archive recovery: streaming is low-latency and connection-dependent; archive recovery is durable, batch-y, and the fallback when a replica falls behind.
Replica count is not free — each walsender is a process and a network stream; use cascading replication beyond a handful of nodes.
WAL volume reducers: fewer/larger checkpoints, wal_compression, UNLOGGED tables for scratch data, avoiding blanket UPDATE of unchanged columns, HOT updates via lower fillfactor.
UNLOGGED tables skip WAL entirely and are fast — and are truncated on crash and never appear on any replica.
Beware wal_level = minimal: it enables COPY optimizations but forbids replication and PITR; almost never worth it on a production cluster.
Sizing pg_wal: at least max_wal_size + wal_keep_size + slot slack + archive backlog headroom, on its own volume when I/O matters.
Big transactions hurt everything: one 50 GB DELETE spikes WAL, stalls logical decoding, and lags every replica — batch it.
Latency stack for a sync commit: local fsync + network RTT + standby fsync; measure each with pg_stat_replication's write_lag/flush_lag before blaming the network.
Sharding/multi-master alternatives (Citus, BDR, pglogical) solve write scaling — plain streaming replication scales reads only.
Consistency model summary: single primary + physical replication = strong on the primary, eventual on replicas, monotonic per replica.
Cost model: an async replica is roughly a full copy of the primary's hardware for zero write throughput gain — justify it with reads, DR, or backup offload.

chapters.title: Common Mistakes & Field Checklist
points: Mistake: leaving a stale replication slot after decommissioning a replica — pg_wal grows to 100% and the primary PANICs on out-of-disk.
Mistake: archive_command that returns 0 on failure — archiving silently breaks and PITR is impossible until someone looks.
Mistake: one sync standby with FIRST 1 — every commit hangs the moment that node reboots; always list a spare.
Mistake: hot_standby_feedback = on with long idle-in-transaction sessions on the replica — primary bloat and wraparound pressure.
Mistake: assuming a replica is caught up during failover — check pg_last_wal_replay_lsn() against the primary before promoting.
Mistake: restarting an old primary after failover — it may accept writes and split brain; fence it first, then pg_rewind.
Mistake: logical replication of a table without a primary key — updates and deletes fail with a replica-identity error.
Mistake: applying DDL only on the publisher — the subscriber's apply worker errors and the whole subscription stalls.
Mistake: no monitoring on wal_status = 'lost' — an invalidated slot means that consumer needs a full rebuild, silently.
Mistake: pg_basebackup without -X stream or a slot on a busy primary — the needed WAL is recycled before the backup finishes.
Mistake: relying on max_standby_streaming_delay = -1 in production — one analyst's query pauses replay and the DR replica drifts hours behind.
Checklist query 1 — lag: SELECT application_name, state, sync_state, pg_wal_lsn_diff(pg_current_wal_lsn(), replay_lsn) AS bytes FROM pg_stat_replication;
Checklist query 2 — slot risk: SELECT slot_name, active, wal_status, pg_size_pretty(pg_wal_lsn_diff(pg_current_wal_lsn(), restart_lsn)) FROM pg_replication_slots;
Checklist query 3 — disk: SELECT pg_size_pretty(sum(size)) FROM pg_ls_waldir(); alert well before the volume is full.
Alert set to ship on day one: replica lag bytes and seconds, slot retained WAL, archiver failure count from pg_stat_archiver, and pg_wal directory size.
